bib.title: BERT for Joint Intent Classification and Slot Filling

legacy_report:
SOURCE: BERT for Joint Intent Classification and Slot Filling, Qian Chen, Zhu Zhuo, Wen Wang (Speech Lab, DAMO Academy, Alibaba Group). Preprint, arXiv:1902.10909v1, 28 Feb 2019. Page 1 footnote: "∗Ongoing work."

COVERAGE: 6 of 6 pages; 21,558 of 21,558 chars, including references. Nothing skipped. In quotes, line breaks are collapsed to spaces and the extraction's hyphens and ligatures are kept.

CLAIMS

- claim: Joint BERT beats the best baseline (Slot-Gated) on all three Snips metrics, most of all on frame accuracy.
  number: intent 98.6 vs 97.0; slot F1 97.0 vs 88.8; sentence 92.8 vs 75.5
  setup: Snips test set, 700 utterances; BERT-Base uncased, fine-tuned; single reported score, no variance
  quote: "On Snips, joint BERT achieves intent classiﬁcation accuracy of 98.6% (from 97.0%), slot ﬁlling F1 of 97.0% (from 88.8%), and sentence-level seman- tic frame accuracy of 92.8% (from 75.5%)."
  where: p4, §4.3

- claim: Joint BERT also beats Slot-Gated on ATIS, with a much smaller slot F1 gain.
  number: intent 97.5 vs 94.1; slot F1 96.1 vs 95.2; sentence 88.2 vs 82.6
  setup: ATIS test set, 893 utterances; same model and training setup
  quote: "On ATIS, joint BERT achieves intent classiﬁcation ac- curacy of 97.5% (from 94.1%), slot ﬁlling F1 of 96.1% (from 95.2%), and sentence-level seman- tic frame accuracy of 88.2% (from 82.6%)."
  where: p4, §4.3

- claim: Full results table for all five models (columns: Snips intent/slot/sent, then ATIS intent/slot/sent).
  number: see the rows below
  setup: metrics are intent accuracy, slot F1 and sentence-level frame accuracy, in %. The three baseline rows are not re-run; they are copied from Goo et al.
  quote: "RNN-LSTM (Hakkani-T¨ur et al., 2016) 96.9 87.3 73.2 92.6 94.3 80.7" / "Atten.-BiRNN (Liu and Lane, 2016) 96.7 87.8 74.1 91.1 94.2 78.9" / "Slot-Gated (Goo et al., 2018) 97.0 88.8 75.5 94.1 95.2 82.6" / "Joint BERT 98.6 97.0 92.8 97.5 96.1 88.2" / "Joint BERT + CRF 98.4 96.7 92.6 97.9 96.0 88.6" / "The results for the ﬁrst group of models are cited from Goo et al. (2018)."
  where: p3, Table 2

- claim: Adding a CRF on top makes no meaningful difference. It is slightly worse on all Snips metrics and on ATIS slot F1, and slightly better on ATIS intent and sentence. The authors' explanation is hedged.
  number: Snips 98.4/96.7/92.6; ATIS 97.9/96.0/88.6
  setup: CRF replaces the softmax slot classifier on joint BERT. My arithmetic: the intent differences are about 1.4 Snips and 3.6 ATIS test utterances.
  quote: "Joint BERT+CRF replaces the softmax classiﬁer with CRF and it performs comparably to BERT, proba- bly due to the self-attention mechanism in Trans- former, which may have sufﬁciently modeled the label structures."
  where: p4 §4.3; numbers p3 Table 2

- claim: Relative frame accuracy gain is large on Snips, which the authors call more complex, and smaller on ATIS. They read this as generalisation from pre-training on mismatched text.
  number: 22.9% relative (Snips); 6.8% relative (ATIS). Both check out against the table.
  setup: against Slot-Gated. The generalisation reading is an interpretation; no experiment isolates it.
  quote: "from 75.5% to 92.8% (22.9% relative). This demonstrates the strong generalization capa- bility of joint BERT model, considering that it is pre-trained on large-scale text from mismatched domains and genres (books and wikipedia)." / "from 82.6% to 88.2% (6.8% relative)."
  where: p4, §4.3

- claim: Ablation (spelled this way in the paper): removing joint learning costs little on Snips.
  number: intent 98.6 to 98.0; slot F1 97.0 to 95.8; no sentence column
  setup: Snips only, 30 epochs. The "No joint" configuration is not described beyond the row; the conclusion calls it BERT models "modeling intent classiﬁcation and slot ﬁlling separately". My arithmetic: 0.6 points is about 4 of 700 utterances.
  quote: "Without joint learning, the accu- racy of intent classiﬁcation drops to 98.0% (from 98.6%), and the slot ﬁlling F1 drops to 95.8% (from 97.0%)." Table row: "No joint 30 98.0 95.8"
  where: p4 §4.4; p3 Table 3

- claim: Epoch sensitivity on Snips: one epoch of fine-tuning already beats the baselines on the two metrics shown, and intent peaks at 20 epochs rather than the reported 30.
  number: epochs: intent/slot = 40: 98.3/96.4; 30: 98.6/97.0; 20: 99.0/96.0; 10: 98.6/96.5; 5: 98.0/95.1; 1: 98.0/93.3
  setup: Snips only; no sentence accuracy. The 30-epoch row equals Table 2's test scores, so Table 3 appears to be test-set numbers (my inference; the paper does not say).
  quote: "Joint BERT 30 98.6 97.0" / "Joint BERT 40 98.3 96.4" / "Joint BERT 20 99.0 96.0" / "Joint BERT 10 98.6 96.5" / "Joint BERT 5 98.0 95.1" / "Joint BERT 1 98.0 93.3"; "The joint BERT model ﬁne-tuned with only 1 epoch already outperforms the ﬁrst group of models in Table 2."
  where: p3 Table 3; p4 §4.4

- claim: Case study: one Snips utterance that Slot-Gated gets wrong on both intent and slots and joint BERT gets right. The authors attribute this, tentatively, to Wikipedia in the pre-training data.
  number: none; a single selected example
  setup: "need to see mother joan of the angels in one second". Gold intent is SearchScreeningEvent, which joint BERT predicts; Slot-Gated predicts BookRestaurant and tags the title as object-name rather than movie-name.
  quote: "because “mother joan of the angels” is a movie entry in Wikipedia. The BERT model was pre-trained partly on Wikipedia and possibly learned this in- formation for this rare phrase."
  where: p4, §4.4 and Table 4

- claim: Dataset sizes and labels; the split is reused from Goo et al.
  number: ATIS 4,478/500/893, 120 slot labels, 21 intents. Snips 13,084/700/700, 72 slot labels, 7 intents.
  setup: train/dev/test utterances; label counts are for the training set
  quote: "We use the same data division as Goo et al. (2018) for both datasets. The training, development and test sets contain 4,478, 500 and 893 utterances, respec- tively. There are 120 slot labels and 21 intent types for the training set." / "The training, development and test sets contain 13,084, 700 and 700 utter- ances, respectively. There are 72 slot labels and 7 intent types for the training set."
  where: p3, §4.1

- claim: Dataset character: ATIS is flight reservations; Snips is from a personal voice assistant and is multi-domain with a larger vocabulary.
  number: none
  setup: as described by the authors; no vocabulary or domain counts given
  quote: "Compared to ATIS, Snips includes multiple do- mains and has a larger vocabulary."
  where: p3 §4.1; p4 §4.3

- claim: Training setup.
  number: 12 layers, 768 hidden, 12 heads; max length 50; batch 128; Adam at 5e-5; dropout 0.1
  setup: English uncased BERT-Base, pre-trained on BooksCorpus and English Wikipedia; hyperparameters tuned on the dev set
  quote: "We use English uncased BERT-Base model 1, which has 12 layers, 768 hidden states, and 12 heads. BERT is pre-trained on BooksCorpus (800M words) (Zhu et al., 2015) and English Wikipedia (2,500M words). For ﬁne-tuning, all hyper-parameters are tuned on the development set. The maximum length is 50. The batch size is 128. Adam (Kingma and Ba, 2014) is used for op- timization with an initial learning rate of 5e-5. The dropout probability is 0.1. The maximum number of epochs is selected from [1, 5, 10, 20, 30, 40]."
  where: p3, §4.2

- claim: Architecture: the intent is a softmax over the [CLS] hidden state, slots are per-word softmaxes over the first WordPiece sub-token, and the joint objective is the product of those probabilities, trained end to end with cross-entropy.
  number: none
  setup: single-label intent per utterance (eq. 1)
  quote: "use the hidden state corresponding to the ﬁrst sub-token as input to the softmax classiﬁer." / "The model is ﬁne- tuned end-to-end via minimizing the cross-entropy loss."
  where: p2-3, §3.2

LIMITS
Conceded by the authors:
- The future work is other datasets and external knowledge: "Future work in- cludes evaluations of the proposed approach on other large-scale and more complex NLU datasets, and exploring the efﬁcacy of combining external knowledge with BERT." (p4)
- It is marked "Ongoing work" (p1).
- The CRF and Wikipedia explanations are hedged ("probably", "may have", "possibly").

What the paper does not show:
- No significance test, confidence interval, seed count or variance, although it says "significant" throughout. The word is not backed by any test.
- Baselines were not re-run. Their numbers are copied from Goo et al., so any run-to-run or implementation differences are uncontrolled.
- The ablation covers Snips only, with no ATIS run and no sentence accuracy. The conclusion's general claim that joint beats separate rests on that one comparison of two metrics (p4).
- No ablation of pre-training: no BERT from random initialisation, and no frozen encoder. The generalisation claim is therefore inferred from the baseline gap and one anecdote.
- No training-size sweep or rare-word analysis, although the abstract frames the problem as small labelled data and rare words.
- No per-slot, per-intent or systematic error analysis; the case is one hand-selected example.
- No latency, model size, memory, training cost or deployment data.
- No out-of-scope, multi-intent or multi-turn evaluation, and no dialogue context.
- No robustness test on speech-recognition errors. ATIS is described as "audio recordings", but the paper does not say what text was evaluated.
- English only, two benchmarks.
- The selection metric for the epoch count is not stated. Table 3 shows intent at 99.0 at 20 epochs against the reported 98.6 at 30.

Dated: the comparison set stops at 2018 RNN models. Nothing here covers LLMs, and the paper predates the DIET comparison and the "solved datasets" caveat already in the note.

CODE: none. The only link is https://github.com/google-research/bert (p3 footnote), which is Google's BERT repository; the paper links no code of its own. Equations, with extraction flattening repaired only in the sub/superscripts: y^i = softmax(W^i h_1 + b^i) (1); y^s_n = softmax(W^s h_n + b^s), n ∈ 1…N (2); p(y^i, y^s|x) = p(y^i|x) ∏_{n=1}^{N} p(y^s_n|x) (3). (p2-3)

FIGURES
- Figure 1, p2: "A high-level view of the proposed model. The input query is “play the song little robin redbreast”." It is the only figure. It shows one encoder with an intent output at [CLS] and slot labels at each token, including how WordPiece sub-tokens align with labels, faster than prose.
- Tables are not figures, but are the most reusable items: Table 2 (p3, all metrics), Table 3 (p3, ablation and epochs), Table 4 (p4, case study), Table 1 (p1, query to semantic frame).

PROBLEMS
- No embedded instructions found.
- Extraction faults:
  - Table 2's header is merged ("Models Snips ATISIntent Slot Sent Intent Slot Sent"); the column order was confirmed against the prose on p4.
  - Table 1's underscores are lost and its slot row is run together ("genre = moviedirected by = Steven Spielberg"), so check it visually before reuse.
  - Figure 1's text is scrambled.
  - Equation sub/superscripts are flattened.
- "Ablation" is the paper's own spelling, not an extraction fault.
- Prose on p3 lists the metrics as slot, intent, sentence, whereas the Table 2 columns are intent, slot, sentence.

Possible conflicts with the target note, for the caller to resolve (line 125 of /Users/ramsey-wise/workspace/learn-ai-engineering/generative-ai/07-agentic-applications/notes/06-application-patterns.md). I did not check Goo et al. itself.
- The note gives Goo's ATIS frame accuracy as "78.9% to 82.2%". Chen's Table 2, citing Goo, gives Slot-Gated ATIS Sent as 82.6.
- The note says slot F1 "moved by 0.6 and 1.0 points". Chen's table gives Atten.-BiRNN to Slot-Gated as 94.2 to 95.2 on ATIS and 87.8 to 88.8 on Snips, so 1.0 on both.
- Goo may report more than one variant or a different figure, so read Goo's table before changing anything. The note's 75.5 and 74.1 for Snips and 78.9 for ATIS do match Chen's table.
